meaning: Sentence-ending particle. Tells the listener something they don't know, or adds force to a warning or invitation.
connection: Sentence (plain form / です・ます form) + よ

senses.label: Giving new information
senses.meaning: Tells the listener something they don't know yet, like “you know” or “I'm telling you”. The speaker is sure; the listener may not know.
senses.connection: Plain form / です・ます form + よ (nouns and na-adjectives often take 「〜だよ」 / 「〜ですよ」)
examples: The ramen at this shop is really good, you know.
It's going to rain tomorrow.
The station is over there.

senses.label: Reminder / warning
senses.meaning: Calls the listener's attention to something. The tone is fairly strong. Common for danger, being late, and so on.
senses.connection: Plain form of verbs / adjectives + よ
examples: Watch out!
If you don't hurry, you'll be late.

senses.label: Invitation / urging
senses.meaning: After 「〜う／〜よう」, 「〜ましょう」 or 「〜て」, it makes an invitation or request stronger. It can sound a little pleading or pushy.
senses.connection: Volitional form / 〜ましょう / 〜て + よ
examples: Come on, let's go together.
Hey, wait a second.
Come on, let's go home now.

senses.label: 「よね」 for checking
senses.meaning: 「よね」 shows that the speaker believes something and asks the listener to confirm it. It carries more of the speaker's own judgment than 「ね」 alone.
senses.connection: Plain form / です・ます form + よね
examples: Tomorrow's a day off, right?
That movie was fun, wasn't it?

notes: Using 「よ」 a lot with a superior, a client or an older person (「知っていますよ」, 「違いますよ」) sounds like “let me tell you”, which comes across as lecturing or talking back. With superiors, soften it to 「〜ですね」 or 「〜かと思います」.
Adding 「よ」 to something the listener already knows or has just said sounds impatient. When someone says 「暑いですね」: ✕「暑いですよ」 → ○「そうですね、暑いですね」.
When answering an invitation or offer, 「いいですよ」 usually means “Sure, that's fine”, but a bare 「いいです」 (especially with a falling tone) usually means “No, thanks”. Dropping 「よ」 can flip the meaning.
Attaching 「よ」 directly to a noun or na-adjective (「学生よ」, 「きれいよ」) sounds feminine. The neutral forms are 「学生だよ」 and 「きれいだよ」; politely, 「学生ですよ」.
In 「よね」 for checking, the order is fixed: ✕「ねよ」 → ○「よね」.

daily.title: Recommending a place
daily.description: Recommending a favorite café to a friend.
daily.example: The cake at that café is really good.

daily.title: Reminding family
daily.description: Reminding a family member to take an umbrella before going out.
daily.example: It's going to rain today. Take an umbrella with you.

daily.title: Hurrying a friend
daily.description: A friend is dawdling, so you tell them to hurry.
daily.example: Come on, let's go. The movie's starting.

work.title: Telling a coworker
work.description: Letting a coworker know the meeting room has changed.
work.example: Today's meeting is on the third floor.

work.title: Informing a customer
work.description: A clerk tells a customer the opening hours.
work.example: This shop is open until ten.

etymology: 「よ」 is an old particle of exclamation and calling out, used for emphasis, as in 「少納言よ」 (“O Shōnagon!”). Later it came to be used mostly at the end of sentences to inform and emphasize.
formation: 「よ」 is an independent sentence-ending particle that is, at heart, a call for attention, like “Hey, listen.” Putting it at the end of a sentence gives the whole sentence that “hey, listen” direction: the speaker pushes the statement toward the listener. So saying something the listener doesn't know with 「よ」 becomes “informing”; saying it about danger or being late becomes a “reminder / warning”; and after the volitional 「〜う」 or the request form 「〜て」 it becomes urging: “Come on, let's…” / “Come on, please…”. Because its essence is “pushing the words toward the listener”, it points the opposite way from 「ね」, which pulls the words back into the space the two people share. In 「よね」 the speaker first shows their own judgment (「よ」) and then asks for agreement (「ね」), which is why the order is fixed.

similar.title: 〜ね
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and the most common comparison: both are sentence-ending particles. 「よ」 hands the listener information they don't have; 「ね」 seeks agreement or confirms something both people know. 「暑いですね」 is sharing a feeling; 「暑いですよ」 is warning the listener, “It's hot out there.”

similar.title: 〜なあ・〜な (exclamation)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are sentence-ending particles that express feeling. 「なあ」 is more like an exclamation to yourself (「きれいだなあ」) and isn't necessarily aimed at anyone; 「よ」 is always aimed at the listener, to inform or remind them.

meaning: Marks the end point of time, place or a continuing action: “until, up to, as far as ...”. It can also pick out an extreme or unexpected example: “even ..., so much as ...”.
connection: Noun／verb dictionary form + まで; noun (+ particle such as に／から／で) + まで

senses.label: End point in time
senses.meaning: Up to a certain time. The action continues during that whole period.
senses.connection: Time noun + まで (〜時まで／〜曜日まで／夜まで)
examples: Yesterday I slept until ten.
I work until five every day.

senses.label: End point in space
senses.meaning: The place a movement reaches, like “to” or “as far as”. Often used with 「行く」, 「歩く」 and 「送る」.
senses.connection: Place noun + まで
examples: I'll walk to the station.
I went to the airport by bus.

senses.label: Until something happens
senses.meaning: Keep doing something until another event happens. The verb before it is in dictionary form.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + まで
examples: Let's wait here until the rain stops.
I read it again and again until I understood.

senses.label: Extreme example
senses.meaning: Picks the least likely example: “even ...”. The hidden message is “so of course everything else, too”. Often used for things that surprise the speaker.
senses.connection: Noun + まで (「が」 and 「を」 are usually dropped); often used with 「〜てしまう」 or 「〜とは」
examples: Even children know it.
Even my best friend doubts me.
Even that gentle teacher got angry.

senses.label: Adding one more thing
senses.meaning: Adds one more item on top of what is already there: “even ... too”. Often paired with 「〜だけでなく」, 「〜うえに」, or 「〜し」. It stresses that things keep getting worse (or better).
senses.connection: 〜だけでなく／〜うえに、Noun + まで
examples: Not only is it raining, but now there's thunder too.
I got lost, and on top of that I even lost my wallet.
They treated me to a meal, and even gave me a gift.

senses.label: After another particle
senses.meaning: Can follow particles like 「に」, 「から」, or 「で」, as in 「にまで」 or 「からまで」. Shows that an effect reaches an unexpected place or person.
senses.connection: Noun + に／から／で／と + まで
examples: That rumor even spread overseas.
I even get emails from people I don't know.

notes: 「まで」 is followed by an ongoing action (「待つ」, 「働く」, 「寝る」). For one-time actions such as handing something in or arriving, use 「までに」: ✕「金曜日まで出してください」 → ○「金曜日までに出してください」. Get it wrong and “hand it in by Friday” becomes “keep handing it in until Friday”.
After a verb, use the dictionary form, even when talking about the past. Don't use the ta-form: ✕「雨がやんだまで待った」 → ○「雨がやむまで待った」.
With arrival verbs such as 「着く」 and 「入る」, mark the destination with 「に」, not 「まで」: ✕「駅まで着きました」 → ○「駅に着きました」. 「駅まで行きました」 is fine.

After particles like 「に」 or 「から」, 「まで」 goes after the particle: ○「外国にまで広まった」. If you say ✕「外国までに広まった」, it becomes a deadline (“by the time it reached overseas”), which means something completely different.
To say “can't even do the bare minimum”, 「さえ」 or 「すら」 sounds more natural: 「ひらがなさえ書けない」. 「まで」 focuses on stretching the range to an unexpected place, and is mostly used when things keep piling up.

daily.description: A passenger tells the driver where to go.
daily.example: To Tokyo Station, please.

daily.description: A friend is running late, and you say you'll wait.
daily.example: I'll wait until you get here.

daily.description: Asking a clerk what time the shop closes.
daily.example: What time is this shop open until?

daily.title: Complaining to a friend
daily.description: When bad luck keeps coming, 「まで」 stresses that things keep getting worse.
daily.example: The train was late, and someone even stole my umbrella.

daily.title: Thanking a friend
daily.description: Visiting a friend who prepared everything with care, you express happy surprise.
daily.example: You even made a cake for me yourself?

work.description: Telling a new coworker about the work hours.
work.example: Work is from nine to six.

work.title: Seeing off a visitor

work.example: I'll take you to the station.

work.example: This trouble even caused inconvenience to our business partners.

work.description: Thanking someone for paying attention to every detail.
work.example: Thank you for considering even the smallest details.

etymology: 「まで」 is a particle for the end of a range, already found in Old Japanese. One theory ties it to 「真手（まて）」, but its origin is not settled.
formation: 「まで」 is an adverbial particle that draws a “limit line”. After a time or place noun it marks the end point of an action, so a continuing verb (待つ・歩く・働く) follows. After a dictionary-form verb, the occurrence of an event becomes the end point, “keep doing ... until ...”; since that moment has not yet arrived, the dictionary form is used, not the ta-form. Pushing the limit to a place it should never reach (even a child, even the wind) gives “even ..., so much as ...”, with the implication that everything nearer is a given. This is why it often pairs with 「だけでなく」 and 「うえに」, and can follow 「に」 or 「から」 (「外国にまで」). Adding 「に」 to make 「までに」 turns “continuing up to the end point” into “completed by some point before it”, which is why the two must not be mixed up.

similar.title: 〜までに
similar.explanation: Same origin: formed by adding 「に」 to 「まで」. 「まで」 means an action continues up to a point (「五時まで働く」); 「までに」 means a one-time action is completed before that point (「五時までに帰る」). Mixing them up turns “until” into “by”.

similar.title: 〜から〜まで
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「まで」 paired with the starting point 「から」 forms a range frame. 「まで」 alone gives only the end point; 「から〜まで」 gives both start and end: 「九時から五時まで働く」.

similar.title: 〜さえ
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both mean “even ...”. 「さえ」 stresses even the most basic thing (often with negative content: 「水さえ飲めない」); 「まで」 stresses that the range reaches somewhere unexpected and is often used to add one more thing: 「雷まで鳴り出した」.

similar.title: 〜すら
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「すら」 works almost like 「さえ」, but it is more formal and stiffer, and is mostly used with negatives: 「名前すら知らない」. 「まで」 is common in both speech and writing and focuses on “adding up to the extreme”.

similar.title: 〜だって (even / also)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「だって」 is conversational and focuses on “even X is no exception” (「子どもだって知っている」); 「まで」 focuses on “even this got added”, with a sense of surprise.

meaning: Shows the start and end of a range in time, space, or things. Like “from ... to ...”.
connection: Noun A + から + Noun B + まで

senses.label: Time range
senses.meaning: From one time to another. Common for opening hours, class times, holidays, and so on.
senses.connection: Time noun + から + time noun + まで
examples: The bank is open from nine to three.
I work from Monday to Friday.

senses.label: Distance range
senses.meaning: From one place to another. Often used with 「歩く」, 「行く」 and 「かかる」.
senses.connection: Place noun + から + place noun + まで
examples: It's a ten-minute walk from my house to the station.
I went from Tokyo to Osaka by shinkansen.

senses.label: Range of things / numbers
senses.meaning: Gives both ends of a range and stresses that everything in between is included.
senses.connection: Noun + から + noun + まで
examples: Please read from page one to page ten.
Everyone from children to adults can enjoy it.

notes: 「から」 marks a starting point only after a noun. After the te-form (「食べてから」) it means “after …”, and after the plain form (「雨だから」) it gives a reason. The three meanings are completely different.
If the end of the range is a deadline, use 「までに」: ✕「三時まで来てください」 → ○「三時までに来てください」. Use 「から〜まで」 only for ongoing actions.
When the range modifies a noun, don't drop 「までの」: ✕「東京から大阪の距離」 → ○「東京から大阪までの距離」.

daily.description: Friends talk about how long it takes to get to school.
daily.example: How long does it take from your house to school?

daily.title: Talking about vacation
daily.description: Telling a friend when your vacation is.
daily.example: Summer vacation is from July 20 to August 31.

daily.title: Checking opening hours
daily.description: Reading the hours posted at a shop entrance.
daily.example: This shop is open from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

work.title: Announcing a meeting
work.description: Telling coworkers the meeting schedule.
work.example: The meeting is from two to three.

work.title: Assigning a task
work.description: A boss tells you which items to check.
work.example: Please check numbers one through twenty.

etymology: 「から」 was originally a case particle for “via” or “starting point”, and 「まで」 marked the end limit. Together they became a fixed frame for the two ends of a range.
formation: 「から」 marks the starting point (where you set out from), and 「まで」 marks the limit at the end (where you stop). Mark the start once and the end once, and whatever lies between them is a “range”, which can be a stretch of time, a distance or a span of numbers. Because both ends are clearly marked, the frame gives a sense of “clear boundaries, everything between them included”, so 「子どもから大人まで」 comes to mean “everyone, young and old”. Each particle can be used on its own; only together do they form “from … to …”. The whole range works like a noun, so it can take 「です」 directly as a predicate, and it takes 「の」 when it modifies a noun: 「東京から大阪までの距離」.

similar.title: 〜から (starting point)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the first half of this pattern. Use 「から」 alone when you give only the starting point: 「授業は九時から始まります」.

similar.title: 〜まで (end point)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the second half of this pattern. Use 「まで」 alone when you give only the end point: 「五時まで働きます」.

similar.title: 〜から〜にかけて
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: it also expresses a range “from … to …”, but the boundaries are vague. It's common in weather forecasts and news (「今夜から明日にかけて雨が降る」). 「から〜まで」 has clear boundaries, so it suits things that need precision, such as opening hours or the material covered by an exam.

meaning: Picks a few examples from a larger group and hints that there are others. Like “A, B, and so on”.
connection: Noun A + や + Noun B + など

senses.label: Listing examples
senses.meaning: Names only some examples and suggests there are more. 「など」 can be followed by particles like 「が」, 「を」 and 「に」.
senses.connection: Noun + や + noun + など (+ が／を／に)
examples: There are books, notebooks and so on on the desk.
I bought apples, bananas and other things at the supermarket.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: 「〜や〜などの + noun」 means “... such as A and B”. It explains a category with concrete examples.
senses.connection: Noun + や + noun + などの + noun
examples: I like sports such as tennis and soccer.
I traveled to old towns like Kyoto and Nara.

senses.label: Gentle suggestion
senses.meaning: Offers a few options for the listener to choose from, in a soft tone. Often used with 「はどうですか」 or 「はいかがですか」.
senses.connection: Noun + や + noun + などは + どうですか
examples: Would you like some tea or coffee?
How about a movie or some shopping this weekend?

notes: 「や」 can only join nouns: ✕「食べるや飲むなど」 → to list actions, use ○「食べたり飲んだりする」.
Mixing up 「と」 and 「や」 changes the information: 「りんごとバナナを買った」 = I bought only these two; 「りんごやバナナを買った」 = I bought other things too. When a list or instructions must be complete, use 「と」.
「など」 after a person can sound dismissive, like “the likes of …” (「あの人などに頼まない」). Used about yourself (「私などには無理です」), it's humble, but never use it about a superior or a client.

daily.title: Talking about local specialties
daily.description: Telling a friend about the good food in your hometown.
daily.example: My town is famous for things like udon and sweets.

daily.title: Talking about your days off
daily.description: Saying what you do on days off when introducing yourself.
daily.example: On my days off, I do things like cooking and cleaning.

work.title: Listing things to bring
work.description: Telling meeting participants what to bring.
work.example: Please bring your laptop, materials and so on.

work.title: Introducing the company
work.description: Telling a client about your company's products.
work.example: Our company makes bags, shoes and other products.

etymology: 「や」 was originally a particle of exclamation or question, and later became a listing particle. 「など」 is generally thought to come from 「なにと」 (“and what-not”), a way of summing up examples.
formation: 「や」 is a listing particle that “picks out a few” nouns and sets them side by side. 「など」 is generally thought to come from 「なにと」 (“something like what”) and means “and so on”. 「や」 gives a few representative items, and 「など」 adds the tail “and others too”; together they mean “… and … and so on”. Because 「や」 itself already implies “just picking a few”, 「本やノート」 still hints at other things even without 「など」. And because 「など」 carries the vague feeling of “just an example, nothing definite”, it can soften a suggestion (「お茶などいかがですか」), leaving the listener room to choose. The same “just an example” nuance, attached to a person, can turn dismissive.

similar.title: 〜と (and / with)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and the most common comparison: 「と」 lists every item (「りんごとバナナ」 = just these two); 「や〜など」 gives only representative examples and hints there are others.

similar.title: 〜とか〜とか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: it also lists examples, but 「とか」 is more casual and can also join verbs and clauses (「歌うとか踊るとか」). 「や」 only joins nouns and works in both writing and speech.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both list examples. 「や〜など」 lists nouns; 「たり〜たりする」 lists actions: 「週末は映画を見たり買い物をしたりします」.

similar.title: 〜なんか・〜など (belittling)
similar.explanation: Same origin: it's the same 「など」. After a person or thing it can mean “something like … (not worth mentioning)”, belittling others or humbling yourself: 「私なんかには無理です」. The 「など」 in 「や〜など」 is a neutral “and so on”.

meaning: Compares two things and says B is more ... than A. Like “B is more ... than A”.
connection: Noun A + より + Noun B + のほうが + adjective, etc.

senses.label: Comparing nouns
senses.meaning: Says B is better, bigger, etc. than A in some way. The focus is on B. Often used to answer a 「どちらが」 question.
senses.connection: Noun A + より + Noun B + のほうが + adjective
examples: The train is faster than the bus.
This year is hotter than last year.
I like black tea more than coffee.

senses.label: Reversed order
senses.meaning: You can also say B first: 「BのほうがAより〜」. The meaning is the same, with even more focus on B.
senses.connection: Noun B + のほうが + Noun A + より + adjective
examples: The train is faster than the bus.
My younger sister is taller than me.

senses.label: Comparing actions
senses.meaning: Compares two ways of doing something. Verbs attach directly to 「より」 and 「ほうが」, with no 「の」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + より + verb dictionary form + ほうが
examples: Walking is quicker than taking the bus.
Cooking at home is cheaper than eating out.

notes: The item before 「より」 is the one that loses. The order is the opposite of English “A is more … than B”: 「AよりBのほうが高い」 = B is more expensive. Reverse the order and you reverse the conclusion.
After a noun, add 「の」 before 「ほう」; verbs and adjectives connect directly: ✕「電車ほうが」 → ○「電車のほうが」; ✕「歩くのほうが」 → ○「歩くほうが」.
Here 「方」 is read 「ほう」, not 「かた」. 「こちらの方（かた）」 means “this person”, while 「こちらの方（ほう）が安い」 means “this one is cheaper”. Misreading it changes the meaning.
Comparing people in front of them (「田中さんより山田さんのほうが上手ですね」) embarrasses the one who comes off worse. In Japan, rating people this directly is considered tactless.

daily.title: Choosing a drink
daily.description: Saying what you'd prefer when a friend asks.
daily.example: I'd rather have tea than juice.

daily.title: Comparing seasons
daily.description: Talking with a friend about your favorite season.
daily.example: I like winter more than summer.

daily.title: Choosing how to get there
daily.description: Discussing how to get to the station.
daily.example: The train is quicker than a taxi.

work.title: Comparing plans
work.description: Telling your boss in a meeting which plan is better.
work.example: Plan B is cheaper than Plan A.

work.title: Recommending a product
work.description: A clerk recommends a product to a customer.
work.example: This one is lighter than that one.

etymology: 「より」 originally means “from”, marking the base of comparison. 「ほう（方）」 originally means “direction” or “side”, so 「Bのほう」 is “B's side”. Together they mean “compared with A, B's side is more ...”.
formation: 「より」 originally means “from”; in comparisons it means “measuring with A as the starting point”, in other words the standard of comparison. 「ほう（方）」 originally means “direction, side”, so 「Bのほう」 is “B's side”. Put them together and add 「が＋adjective」, and the literal meaning is “taking A as the standard, B's side is more …”. Because 「ほう」 divides things into “this side” and “that side”, the pattern naturally compares only two things; for three or more, switch to 「〜の中で〜がいちばん」. 「ほう」 is a noun, so a noun modifying it needs 「の」 (「電車のほう」), while verbs and adjectives can already modify nouns directly and take no 「の」 (「歩くほう」, 「大きいほう」).

similar.title: 〜は〜より〜 (comparison)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「AはBより〜」 talks about A as the topic (「電車はバスより速い」); 「AよりBのほうが」 puts the focus on the winner B and is often used to answer an either-or question.

similar.title: 〜と〜とどちらが
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: this is the question form for comparing two things, and 「〜より〜のほうが」 is its standard answer: 「犬と猫とどちらが好き？」 — 「猫より犬のほうが好き」.

similar.title: 〜ほど〜ない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: it also compares two things, but says negatively that “A is not as … as B”: 「バスは電車ほど速くない」. 「より〜のほうが」 says positively that B comes out ahead.

similar.title: 〜ほうがいい
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「ほう（方）」 to split the choices into “this side / that side”. 「〜たほうがいい」 is advice that follows a comparison, “you'd better …” (「早く寝たほうがいい」); 「より〜のほうが」 only states the result of a comparison.

meaning: Asks which of two things is more ... . Like “Which is more ..., A or B?”.
connection: Noun A + と + Noun B + と + どちらが + adjective, etc. + か

senses.label: Choosing between two
senses.meaning: Asks the listener to pick the one of two that fits better. 「どちら」 is the polite word. Answer with 「〜のほうが〜」.
senses.connection: Noun A + と + Noun B + と + どちらが + adjective / 好き, etc. + ですか
examples: Which do you like better, dogs or cats?
Which is faster, the bus or the train?

senses.label: Setting the scope with 「では」
senses.meaning: 「AとBとでは」 or 「AとBでは」 first sets up what's being compared, then asks which is more ... . A bit more formal.
senses.connection: Noun A + と + Noun B + (と)では + どちらが
examples: Which is bigger, Tokyo or Osaka?
Which do you like better, summer or winter?

senses.label: Casual 「どっち」
senses.meaning: In casual speech, use 「どっち」. The second 「と」 is often dropped and replaced by a pause. You can also use 「に」 or 「を」 to ask about a choice.
senses.connection: Noun A + と + Noun B、どっちが／どっちに／どっちを
examples: Coffee or tea, which do you want?
Ramen or curry, which will you have?

notes: You can't use 「どちら」 for three or more: ✕「りんごとみかんとぶどうとどちらが好き？」 → ○「この中でどれ（何）がいちばん好き？」.
Don't use 「いちばん」 when answering a comparison of two: ✕「猫がいちばん好きです」 → ○「猫のほうが好きです」.
When asking a guest or superior to choose, 「どっち」 sounds too casual; use 「どちら」. Even more politely: 「どちらになさいますか」, 「どちらがよろしいですか」.
「どちら」 is also the polite form of 「どこ」 and 「だれ」: 「どちら様ですか」 means “May I ask who's calling?” and 「お国はどちらですか」 means “Which country are you from?”, not “which of the two”.

etymology: 「どちら」 is made from the question element 「ど」 plus 「ちら」, which shows direction. It first meant “which direction”, then “which of the two”. 「どっち」 is its casual sound change.
formation: 「と」 is a listing particle. 「AとBと」 sets the two options side by side, and the second 「と」 “closes” the list, showing there are just these two. 「どちら」 is the question element 「ど」 plus 「ちら」, which marks direction, so its original meaning is “which direction”. Two options are like two directions in front of you, so asking “which direction” means asking “which of the two”. Then 「が」 raises “which one” as the subject, followed by an adjective and 「か」 to make a question. Because 「どちら」 points to only one of two directions, the pattern is limited to choosing between two. Inserting 「では」 (「AとBとでは」) first fences off the scope of the comparison and then asks, so it sounds more formal.

similar.title: 〜より〜のほうが
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: this is the standard pattern for answering 「どちらが」: 「犬より猫のほうが好きです」. Ask with 「どちら」, answer with 「ほう」.

similar.title: 〜の中で〜がいちばん
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: also a comparison question, but for three or more: 「果物の中で何がいちばん好きですか」. When asking “which one” between two, only 「どちら」 works.

similar.title: 〜これ・それ・あれ・どれ
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「どれ」 and 「どちら」 are both 「ど」 question words in the 「こそあど」 system. 「どれ」 is for choosing among three or more; 「どちら」 is only for two.

meaning: Points out the one that is the most ... within a group of three or more. Like “the most ... of all ...”.
connection: Noun (group) + の中で + Noun + が + いちばん + adjective, etc.

senses.label: The most ... in a group
senses.meaning: First set the group with 「の中で」, then say which is “the most ...”. The group usually has three or more members.
senses.connection: Noun (group) + の中で + Noun + が + いちばん + adjective
examples: Of all sports, I like soccer the best.
In my family, my father is the tallest.

senses.label: Question form
senses.meaning: Asks which is the most ... in a group. Choose the question word by type: 「何／どれ」 for things, 「誰」 for people, 「どこ」 for places, 「いつ」 for times.
senses.connection: Noun (group) + の中で + 何／どれ／誰／どこ／いつ + が + いちばん
examples: Which fruit do you like best?
Who is the fastest in the class?
When is the busiest time of the year?

senses.label: 「〜でいちばん」
senses.meaning: When the group is a place or organization, you can drop 「の中」 and just use 「で」. Often used to modify a noun.
senses.connection: Noun (place / group) + で + いちばん + adjective
examples: Mt. Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan.
This is the most popular dish at this restaurant.

notes: You can't use 「いちばん」 between two: ✕「犬と猫の中で犬がいちばん好き」 → ○「犬と猫では犬のほうが好き」.
Mark the range with 「で」, not 「に」: ✕「クラスの中に誰がいちばん速いですか」 → ○「クラスの中で」.
When asking about three or more, you can't use 「どちら」: ✕「スポーツの中でどちらがいちばん好き？」 → ○「何がいちばん好き？」.
In reports, news and explanatory writing, 「いちばん」 sounds conversational; use 「最も」 instead: 「日本で最も高い山」.

etymology: 「一番」 originally means “number one, first place”, and came to be used as the adverb “most”. 「中」 means “inside a range”, and 「で」 marks the range.
formation: 「の中」 means “inside …”. Add 「で」, which marks a range, and 「〜の中で」 means “within this group”: it first draws a circle around the members being compared. 「が」 points out the one chosen, putting the focus on “which one / who”. 「いちばん（一番）」 originally means “number one”; used as an adverb it means “in first place”, that is, “most”. So the whole pattern means “within this group, number one is X”. Being number one requires a crowd of candidates, so the range usually has three or more members. When the range itself is a place or a group, “inside” goes without saying, so 「の中」 is dropped and you just say 「〜でいちばん」.

similar.title: 〜と〜とどちらが
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are question patterns for comparison. Use 「AとBとどちらが」 for two things; use 「〜の中で〜がいちばん」 only for three or more.

similar.title: 〜より〜のほうが
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: the pattern for stating the result of comparing two (the comparative): 「AよりBのほうが〜」. This entry is the superlative for three or more.

similar.title: 〜ほど〜はない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「AほどBはない」 also means “A is the most …” (「富士山ほど美しい山はない」), but it uses a negative form and carries the speaker's personal emotion; 「いちばん」 plainly states what comes first.

meaning: Links two clauses to show contrast. It is also used to lead into a topic or to end a sentence softly. Like “but” or “although”.
connection: Plain form / です・ます form + けど・けれど・けれども

senses.label: Contrast
senses.meaning: The two parts go against each other or don't match, like “..., but ...” or “although ...”.
senses.connection: Plain form / です・ます form + けど、〜
examples: This restaurant is expensive, but the food is good.
Japanese is difficult, but it's interesting.

senses.label: Lead-in to a topic
senses.meaning: Gives an opening phrase before making a request or asking a question. There is no sense of contrast here.
senses.connection: 〜んです / すみません, etc. + けど、〜
examples: Excuse me, do you have a moment?
It's about next week's meeting. Does the time work for you?

senses.label: Soft sentence ending
senses.meaning: Leaves off the second half and ends with 「けど」. It sounds soft and lets the listener fill in the rest. Common when declining or saying something is difficult.
senses.connection: 〜んです / 〜です + けど……
examples: I have something to do, so...
That would be a bit difficult...

senses.label: At the start of a sentence
senses.meaning: 「だけど」 or 「けど」 at the start of a sentence means “but”. Casual.
senses.connection: Sentence start: だけど、〜／けど、〜
examples: I want to go. But I don't have any money.

notes: After a noun or na-adjective, you must add 「だ」 or 「です」 first: ✕「雨けど」, 「静かけど」 → ○「雨だけど」, 「静かですけど」.
Don't use 「けど」 in business emails, reports or papers; it sounds casual. In writing use 「が」; in formal speech use 「けれども」.

「行きたいんですけど……」 and 「ちょっと難しいんですけど……」 are usually polite refusals in Japan. Don't take them as “I want to go” or “it's a bit hard but doable” and keep pressing. When you need to refuse, saying it this way is also more tactful than a flat 「行けません」.

etymology: 「けれども」 is generally thought to come from 「けれ」, a form of the classical auxiliary 「けり」, plus the conjunctive particle 「ども」. It was later shortened to 「けれど」 and 「けど」.
formation: 「けれども」 is generally thought to be 「けれ」 (the realis form of the classical auxiliary 「けり」) plus the conjunctive particle 「ども」. 「ども」 after the realis form means “although it is already so, still …”: it first admits the first clause as fact, then brings in something that doesn't fit with it. That is where the “but” meaning comes from. This structure, “first admit one thing, then keep going”, doesn't have to be a contrast: throw out an opening line first (「すみませんけど」) and then make a request, and it becomes a lead-in; cut off the second half entirely, keep only the “admitting” part and let the listener fill in the rest, and it becomes the soft sentence-final use (often for refusing). 「けれど」 and 「けど」 are progressively shortened forms; the shorter, the more casual.

similar.title: 〜が (contrast: but)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and interchangeable: 「が」 is more written and formal, suitable for reports and emails; 「けど」 leans conversational. The lead-in use works the same way, and 「すみませんが」 is more polite than 「すみませんけど」.

similar.title: 〜のに (contrast)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: it also expresses contrast, but 「のに」 carries surprise, frustration or regret (「約束したのに来なかった」); 「けど」 is a neutral “but”. Also, 「のに」 can't be followed by a request or an intention.

similar.title: 〜でも (at the start of a sentence: but)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「でも」 goes at the start of the second sentence (「高い。でも、おいしい」); 「けど」 attaches to the end of the first sentence and joins the two into one.

similar.title: 〜んですが (lead-in)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: it matches the lead-in use of 「けど」. 「〜んですが」 is more polite and suits superiors and clients: 「ちょっとお聞きしたいんですが」.

meaning: 「でも」 has three common uses: at the start of a sentence it marks contrast (“but”); after a noun it gives an example to soften an invitation or suggestion (“or something”); after a question word it means “any-” (“whatever / whoever ~”).
connection: Sentence-initial: sentence. + でも、sentence; noun (+ particle) + でも + 〜ませんか／〜ましょう／〜たい; question word (何・誰・どこ・いつ etc.) / どんな + noun + でも
etymology: All three uses come from 「で」 (the connective form of the copula 「だ」) + 「も」 (a topic-highlighting particle), originally meaning “even if it is ~”. Sentence-initial 「でも」 is generally thought to be 「それでも」 with 「それ」 dropped; after a noun it means “even ~ would do”, which weakened into giving an example; after a question word it means “even any one of them”, giving the “any-” sense.
formation: 「でも」 = 「で」 (the te-form of 「だ」) + 「も」, literally “even if it is ~”. At the start of a sentence it first concedes what was just said and then states something that does not fit it (“even so, ~”), which gives contrast; after a noun it means “even this would be fine”, demoting it to a casual example, which makes invitations and suggestions sound gentle; a question word stands for “any one not yet decided”, and adding 「でも」 means “it holds whichever you plug in”, giving the “any-” sense. The three share one origin and are told apart by position (sentence start / after a noun / after a question word) and by what follows.

senses.label: Contrast
senses.meaning: After one sentence, start the next with 「でも」 to say something opposite or unexpected. Common in speech.
examples: This outfit is cute. But it's a little expensive.
I studied really hard. But I did badly on the exam.

senses.label: Excuses / objections
senses.meaning: Disagrees with what the other person said, or gives an excuse. The tone can sound a bit defensive.
senses.connection: (What the other person said) → でも、〜
examples: But I didn't say anything.
But you said yesterday it was fine, didn't you?

senses.label: Soft invitations and suggestions
senses.meaning: Doesn't pin down one thing; it just offers an example to soften the tone, like “... or something”. Often with 「〜ませんか」, 「〜ましょう」 or 「〜よう」.
senses.connection: Noun + でも + 〜ませんか／〜ましょう／〜(よ)う
examples: Would you like some tea or something?
If you're free, let's go see a movie or something.
Shall we go to the park or somewhere?

senses.label: Soft wishes
senses.meaning: When saying what you want or suggesting something, 「でも」 makes it sound less pushy: “... or something like that”.
senses.connection: Noun + でも + 〜たい／〜たら／〜ください
examples: I feel like having something cold to drink.
If you're tired, why not take a little break or something?

senses.label: Any ... at all
senses.meaning: No exceptions; anything fits. Like “anything, anyone, anywhere, anytime”. The predicate is positive.
senses.connection: 何でも／誰でも／どこでも／いつでも／どれでも／どちらでも
examples: I'll eat anything.
Anyone can join this event.
If you're ever in trouble, contact me anytime.

senses.label: どんな + noun
senses.meaning: 「どんな + noun + でも」 means “no matter what kind of ...”, stressing there are no conditions.
senses.connection: どんな + noun + でも
examples: I'll work hard at any kind of job.
Anyone can make mistakes.

notes: Shooting back at a superior or client with 「でも」 (「でも、それは…」) sounds like making excuses or talking back, which is very rude in a Japanese workplace. Accept first, then explain: 「おっしゃる通りですが、実は…」.

Sentence-initial 「でも」 and 「でも」 after a noun mean completely different things: 「お茶でも飲みませんか」 means “How about some tea or something?”, not “but”. The key is whether 「でも」 is at the start of the sentence.
Using 「でも」 for your own choice sounds reluctant: when asked what you'd like to eat, 「ラーメンでもいいです」 sounds like “ramen will do, I guess”, which is impolite. If you want it, say 「ラーメンがいいです」.
Drop 「を」 and 「が」, but keep other particles before 「でも」: ✕「お茶をでも飲みませんか」→ ○「お茶でも飲みませんか」; ○「公園にでも行きましょう」.
Question word + 「でも」 pairs with a positive, question word + 「も」 with a negative; mix them up and the meaning flips: ✕「誰でも来なかった」→ ○「誰も来なかった」; ✕「何も食べます」→ ○「何でも食べます」.

similar.title: 〜しかし (at the start of a sentence: however)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both are sentence-initial words for “but”. 「しかし」 is written and formal, used in texts and speeches; 「でも」 is conversational.

similar.title: 〜か何か
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜か何か」 explicitly says “or something else” (「お茶か何か飲みませんか」); like 「でも」 it leaves room for choice, but it's more colloquial and stresses “not just this”.

similar.title: 〜なんか・〜など (belittling)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「なんか」 can also offer a casual example (「お茶なんかどう？」), but it often has a belittling or self-deprecating tone; in suggestions to superiors, 「でも」 is the safer choice.

similar.title: 〜question word + も〜ない (total negation)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both are “question word + も”. 「何も」 and 「誰も」 add 「も」 directly and pair with a negative: “nothing, nobody”; 「何でも」 and 「誰でも」, with the extra 「で」, pair with a positive: “anything, anyone”.

similar.title: 〜でも〜でも
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「AでもBでも」 lists two items: “whether A or B” (「肉でも魚でも食べる」); this pattern covers everything with a single question word.

meaning: Shows that something or someone exists, like “there is / there are”. Use 「ある」 for inanimate things and 「いる」 for people and animals.
connection: (Place + に) + Noun + が + ある／いる

senses.label: Things
senses.meaning: Says there is something somewhere. Used for things that aren't alive and don't move on their own. Plants also take 「ある」.
senses.connection: Place + に + Noun + が + ある／あります
examples: There's a book on the desk.
There's a convenience store near the station.

senses.label: People / animals
senses.meaning: Says there is a person or animal somewhere. Used for living things that move on their own.
senses.connection: Place + に + Noun + が + いる／います
examples: There are children in the park.
We have two cats at home.

senses.label: Having
senses.meaning: Says someone has something, or has a person in some relationship (family, friends). The person is often marked with 「は」.
senses.connection: Person + は + Noun + が + ある／いる
examples: I have one older brother.
I don't have time today.

senses.label: Events / happenings
senses.meaning: Says an event takes place or something happens. Use 「ある」 even if people take part.
senses.connection: (Place + で) + Noun + が + ある
examples: There's a test tomorrow.
There was an accident in front of the station yesterday.

notes: Use 「いる」 for people and animals, not 「ある」: ✕「家に猫があります」 → ○「猫がいます」. “I have an older brother” is also ○「兄がいます」.
The negative of 「ある」 is 「ない」: ✕「あらない」 → ○「ない」, 「ありません」.
Use 「で」 for where an event takes place: ✕「教室に会議がある」 → ○「教室で会議がある」.
On the phone, when telling a client whether someone from your own company is in, use the humble 「おります」: ○「田中はただいま席におりません」. Using 「いらっしゃる」 to elevate your own colleague is a serious blunder.

etymology: 「ある」 comes from classical 「あり」, meaning “to exist”. 「いる」 comes from classical 「ゐる（居る）」, originally “to sit, to stay”. That is why it came to be used only for living things.
formation: The pattern has three parts: 「に」 marking the place of existence, 「が」 marking what exists, and the existence verb 「ある／いる」. 「が」 pushes “what exists” forward as new information, so the focus of 「NがPにある」 is “what is there”. 「ある」 comes from 「あり」, meaning “to exist”; 「いる」 comes from 「ゐる」, originally “to sit, to stay”. “Staying” needs a subject that can move on its own, so 「いる」 is for people and animals and 「ある」 for everything else. “Having” and “taking place” are both extensions of existence: “an older brother exists on my side” means “I have an older brother”; “something comes into being somewhere” means “it is held / it happens”. Because that is an event, an action, the place is marked with 「で」, the particle for where actions happen.

similar.title: 〜は〜にある・〜は〜にいる (location)
similar.explanation: Same origin and close in meaning: it uses the same 「ある／いる」. 「（place に）Nがある」 focuses on “what is there” (N is the new information); 「Nは（place に）ある」 focuses on “where N is” (the place is the new information).

similar.title: 〜ございます (formal 「ある」)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「ございます」 is the formal version of 「あります」, often used by shop staff to customers and in formal settings: 「お手洗いはあちらにございます」.

similar.title: いらっしゃる・おっしゃる (special honorific verbs)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「いらっしゃる」 is the honorific form of 「いる」, used for superiors and clients: 「部長はいらっしゃいますか」. For yourself or people from your own company, use the humble 「おります」.

meaning: Takes a known person or thing as the topic and says where it is. Like “X is in / at Y”.
connection: Noun + は + place + に + ある／いる

senses.label: Location of things
senses.meaning: Says where a known thing is. The topic takes 「は」 and the place takes 「に」. Use 「ある」 for inanimate things.
senses.connection: Noun + は + place + に + あります
examples: The restroom is on the second floor.
My house is near the station.

senses.label: Location of people / animals
senses.meaning: Says where a person or animal is. Use 「いる」.
senses.connection: Noun + は + place + に + います
examples: My mother is in the kitchen now.
The cat is under the chair.

senses.label: Asking where
senses.meaning: Use 「どこ」 to ask the location. Answer with the same 「〜は〜にあります／います」.
senses.connection: Noun + は + どこ + に + ありますか／いますか
examples: Excuse me, where is the station?
Where is Mr. Tanaka?

notes: Mark the location with 「に」, not 「で」: ✕「母は台所でいます」 → ○「母は台所にいます」.
When asking “where is …?”, mark the topic with 「は」: ✕「駅がどこにありますか」 → ○「駅はどこにありますか」 (「どこ」 is the new information; the thing before it is already known).
When asking where a superior or client is, use honorific language: ✕「社長はどこにいますか」 → ○「社長はどちらにいらっしゃいますか」.
When telling a client where someone from your own company is, use the humble form: ○「田中はただいま会議室におります」. Saying 「いらっしゃいます」 elevates your own colleague, which is very rude.

work.description: Someone comes looking for a person, and you tell them where he is.
work.example: The department manager is in the meeting room now.

etymology: 「は」 was originally a binding particle that marks the topic, and 「に」 marks the place of existence. 「ある」 comes from classical 「あり」, and 「いる」 from 「ゐる（居る）」, originally “to stay there”.
formation: 「は」 raises a person or thing both speakers know as the topic (“as for N …”), and the following 「place＋に＋ある／いる」 explains it: 「に」 marks where it is, and 「ある／いる」 expresses existence. The topic is known, so the new information falls on the place, and the focus of the whole sentence is “where”. This is exactly the reverse of 「（place に）Nがある」, where 「が」 pushes N forward as new information and the focus is “what is there”. Because the focus is the place, speech often drops 「にある／にいる」 and just says 「〜は〜です」.

similar.title: 〜がある・〜がいる (existence)
similar.explanation: Same origin and close in meaning: 「（place に）Nがある」 focuses on “what is there”; 「Nは（place に）ある」 focuses on “where N is”. Use 「が」 for something mentioned for the first time and 「は」 for something already known.

similar.title: 〜だ・〜です
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: in speech, 「〜は〜にあります」 is often shortened to 「〜は〜です」: 「トイレは二階です」. But 「です」 can only replace sentences that say where something is, not existence sentences that say what is there: ✕「机の上に本です」.

similar.title: いらっしゃる・おっしゃる (special honorific verbs)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: when asking where a superior or client is, replace 「いる」 with the honorific 「いらっしゃる」: 「社長はどちらにいらっしゃいますか」.

meaning: 「は」 sets the topic (the “big subject”), and 「が」 then picks out a part of it (the “small subject”) and says something about it; it also covers “experiencer は + object が” for emotion and ability, and “topic は + doer が”.
connection: Noun A + は + noun B + が + predicate (adjective, verb, etc.)

senses.label: Whole and part
senses.meaning: A is the whole, B is a part of A, and the rest describes B. The whole sentence describes A.
senses.connection: Noun (whole) + は + Noun (part) + が + adjective
examples: Elephants have long trunks.
This room has big windows.

senses.label: Body / sensations
senses.meaning: Describes a person's physical features or how their body feels. A is the person, B is a body part.
senses.connection: Person + は + body part + が + adjective
examples: I have a headache.
Mr. Tanaka is tall.

senses.label: Topic and aspect
senses.meaning: A is the topic, and B is the aspect of A being judged. Common when describing shops, cities and so on.
senses.connection: Noun (topic) + は + Noun (aspect) + が + adjective
examples: This shop's ramen is delicious.
Prices are high in Tokyo.

senses.label: Topic + who does it
senses.meaning: 「は」 sets the topic, and the part with 「が」 says something about it. The topic can be the object of the action, a time, a place, and so on. Like “As for A, B ...”.
senses.connection: Noun A + は + noun B + が + verb; e.g. 「この料理は母が作った」
examples: My older brother took this photo.
Today's lunch is on me.

senses.label: Object of feelings and abilities
senses.meaning: With state predicates like 「好き」, 「分かる」, 「欲しい」, 「できる」, the object takes 「が」 and the person who feels takes 「は」.
senses.connection: Person + は + object + が + 好き／分かる／欲しい／できる／怖い
examples: I understand a little Japanese.
My little brother is afraid of dogs.

senses.label: が inside clauses
senses.meaning: The topic of the main sentence takes 「は」, but the subject inside a clause, such as a noun-modifying or conditional clause, usually takes 「が」.
senses.connection: Noun A + は + [noun B + が + verb] + noun + predicate
examples: I like the food my mother makes best.
He said he won't come if it rains.

notes: For bodily sensations say 「私は頭が痛い」, not ✕「私の頭が痛いです」 (which sounds like you're describing someone else's head).
Don't use 「が」 for the outer subject too: 「田中さんは背が高い」 is a plain description, while 「田中さんが背が高い」 becomes “(It's) Tanaka (who) is tall”, stressing Tanaka rather than anyone else.
Don't use 「は」 after a question word: ✕「どこは痛いですか」 → ○「どこが痛いですか」.
In sentences about feelings or ability, 「は」 marks the person who feels and 「が」 marks the object; swap them and the meaning flips: 「私は田中さんが好きだ」 (I like Tanaka) ↔ 「田中さんは私が好きだ」 (Tanaka likes me).
「は」 reaches to the end of the sentence, while 「が」 only covers the predicate right next to it: in 「私は彼が来た時、寝ていた」, the one asleep is “me” and the one who came is “him”.

etymology: In Japanese 「は」 was originally a binding particle that marks contrast or presentation, while 「が」 was a case particle; their jobs differ, so both can appear in one sentence. In Old Japanese 「が」 was often used inside subordinate clauses, and this tradition continues today: the topic takes 「は」, and the subject of a clause or predicate takes 「が」. Such sentences are often called “big subject / small subject” or “double subject” sentences.
formation: This pattern stacks two subject-predicate layers: the outer 「A は + explanation」 and the inner 「B が + predicate」. 「は」 sets A as the topic, “speaking of A”, and its scope runs to the end of the sentence; 「が」 only marks who does the predicate right after it, or for whom it holds. So the whole sentence says “speaking of A, how is its B?”, with the inner 「B が〜」 as a whole explaining A. This is the common source of the three uses: whole and part (象は鼻が長い), body feelings (私は頭が痛い) and aspect of evaluation (この店はラーメンがおいしい). Because it is A that is being described, 「象は鼻が長い」 describes the elephant, not just the trunk. The same structure extends further: when the inner predicate is a stative word such as 「好き」「分かる」「できる」, 「が」 marks the object and 「は」 the experiencer (私は日本語が分かる); when the inner predicate is an action, it becomes “topic + agent” (この料理は母が作った). A clause is just a small description inside and needs no topic of its own, so a clause subject takes 「が」, not 「は」.

similar.title: 〜の (possession / modification)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and the most common comparison: 「象の鼻は長い」 is also correct, but the topic is just “the elephant's trunk”; in 「象は鼻が長い」 the topic is the elephant, and the sentence describes a feature of elephants.

similar.title: 〜が好き・〜が嫌い・〜が上手・〜が下手
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: it is also a two-layer 「AはBが〜」 structure, except that the inner 「が」 marks the object of a liking or skill: 「私は音楽が好きです」.

similar.title: 〜は〜が、〜は〜 (contrast)
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「は」 and 「が」. In a contrast sentence, the two 「は」 set things side by side (「肉は好きだが、魚は嫌いだ」), and the 「が」 there is the conjunction “but”; in this entry, 「が」 is the case particle marking the subject.

similar.title: 〜が (subject)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「が」 alone just describes something happening in front of you (「雨が降っている」); adding 「は」 in front first sets “what we're talking about”, then narrates.

meaning: Says you like, dislike, are good at, or are bad at something. These words are na-adjectives, and the thing is marked with 「が」.
connection: Noun + が + 好き／嫌い／上手／下手 (です)

senses.label: Like / dislike
senses.meaning: 「好き」 means like, 「嫌い」 means dislike. The thing takes 「が」, not 「を」. For stronger feelings, say 「大好き」 or 「大嫌い」.
senses.connection: Noun + が + 好き／嫌い + です
examples: I like cats.
My older brother hates vegetables.
What do you like?

senses.label: Good at / bad at
senses.meaning: 「上手」 means good at, skilled. 「下手」 means bad at, poor at. Mostly used to judge other people's skills.
senses.connection: Noun + が + 上手／下手 + です
examples: My older sister is a good cook.
I'm bad at singing.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: Before a noun, use 「〜が好きな + noun」. Inside this kind of clause, 「が」 can also become 「の」.
senses.connection: Noun + が + 好きな／上手な + noun
examples: I want to make friends with people who like soccer.
My favorite food is sushi.

senses.label: 「得意」・「苦手」
senses.meaning: When talking about your own skills, 「得意」 sounds more modest and natural. 「苦手」 means you're not good at something or don't really like it.
senses.connection: Noun + が + 得意／苦手 + です
examples: I'm good at math.
I'm not good at English.

notes: Mark the object with 「が」, not 「を」: ✕「猫を好きです」 → ○「猫が好きです」.
Calling yourself 「上手です」 sounds boastful; 「得意です」 is better. When someone says 「日本語が上手ですね」, the usual modest reply is 「いえいえ、まだまだです」. Answering 「はい、上手です」 sounds arrogant.
Telling a superior or older person 「〜がお上手ですね」 sounds like you're grading them, which is condescending and considered rude in Japanese business settings. Say 「勉強になります」 or 「さすがです」 instead.
「嫌い」 is very strong. Saying 「嫌いです」 directly about food someone made or something they recommended is hurtful; soften it to 「〇〇はちょっと苦手で……」.
The negative follows the na-adjective pattern: ✕「好きない」 → ○「好きじゃない」, 「好きではありません」.

etymology: 「好き」 comes from the stem of the verb 「好く」, and 「嫌い」 from the stem of 「嫌う」. Both became na-adjectives. 「上手」 and 「下手」 originally meant “upper side” and “lower side”, and came to mean high and low skill.
formation: 「好き」 and 「嫌い」 are na-adjectives that grew out of the continuative forms of the verbs 「好く」 and 「嫌う」; 「上手」 and 「下手」 were originally nouns (“upper side / lower side” → high or low level of skill) and are also used as na-adjectives. They express a “state or quality”, not an “action” done to an object, so they have no true direct object; the object is marked with 「が」. 「猫が好き」 literally means “cats are liked (by me)”. Because they're na-adjectives, they follow na-adjective patterns for the negative and for modifying nouns (「好きじゃない」, 「好きな人」). The whole sentence often takes the two-layer 「AはBが〜」 structure: A is the person who feels or has the skill, and B is the object.

similar.title: 〜のが好き・〜のが上手 (nominalizing verbs)
similar.explanation: Same origin: it uses the same 「好き・上手」. When the object is a noun, say 「Nが好き」 directly; when it's an action, first turn it into a noun with 「の」: 「泳ぐのが好きです」.

similar.title: 〜がわかる・〜ができる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: both 「上手」 and 「できる」 can describe skills. 「英語ができる」 just means “can (use) English”; 「英語が上手」 means “speaks it well”, a higher evaluation.

similar.title: 〜がほしい
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and often learned together: it also marks the object with 「が」 and expresses an inner feeling. 「好き」 is a lasting liking; 「ほしい」 is wanting something right now. For a third person, change it to 「ほしがっている」.

meaning: 「がわかる」 means to understand or know. 「ができる」 means can do or be able to; it also means something is made, built, or ready. Both mark the thing with 「が」.
connection: Noun + が + わかる／できる

senses.label: Understand
senses.meaning: Shows that you understand something or have figured something out. The thing takes 「が」, not 「を」.
senses.connection: Noun + が + わかる／わかります
examples: I understand a little Japanese.
I don't know what this kanji means.
I finally figured out the answer.

senses.label: Can / be able to
senses.meaning: Shows that someone has an ability, or that something can be done somewhere.
senses.connection: Noun + が + できる／できます
examples: My older brother can speak English.
I can't ski.
You can go shopping here.

senses.label: Come into being / be ready
senses.meaning: Something new appears or is built, or something is finished and ready.
senses.connection: Noun + が + できる／できた
examples: A new supermarket opened in front of the station.
Dinner's ready!

notes: Mark the object with 「が」, not 「を」: ✕「日本語をわかります」 → ○「日本語がわかります」.
Saying “understood” to a superior or client: 「わかりました」 is a bit casual, and 「了解です」 is even less appropriate. In formal settings say 「承知しました」 or 「かしこまりました」.
Answering a reminder with 「わかってる」 or 「わかっています」 sounds like “You don't need to tell me, I already know”, which comes across as impatient. When accepting a reminder, say 「はい、気をつけます」.
「できる」 can't attach directly to a verb: ✕「泳ぐができる」 → ○「泳ぐことができる」 or 「泳げる」.

etymology: 「わかる」 comes from 「分く」 (to divide): sorting things out clearly is “understanding”. 「できる」 comes from classical 「出で来（いでく）」, “to come out, to appear”, and later came to mean “to be able to”.
formation: 「わかる」 comes from 「分く」 (to divide): sorting out things that are mixed together is “figuring them out”. 「できる」 comes from 「出で来（いでく）」, “to come out, to appear”: when a task can “come out”, that means “being able to do it”; when a thing “has come out”, it means “it's finished, it's been built”. Both describe a “state that comes about naturally”, not an action the subject deliberately performs on an object, so the object takes 「が」, not 「を」: 「日本語がわかる」 literally means “Japanese is clear (to me)”. For the same reason, since they are state verbs, 「わかっている」 means “already in a state of understanding”, i.e. “I already know”, not “I'm in the middle of understanding”.

similar.title: 〜ことができる
similar.explanation: Same origin: both use 「できる」. A noun connects directly as 「Nができる」 (「スキーができる」); an action needs 「verb dictionary form＋ことができる」 (「泳ぐことができる」).

similar.title: 〜られる・〜える (potential form)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: potential forms such as 「話せる」 and 「読める」 also express ability and are more conversational than 「ことができる」. The object can also take 「が」: 「日本語が話せる」.

similar.title: 〜が好き・〜が嫌い・〜が上手・〜が下手
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「できる」 just says “can do”, while 「上手」 says “does it well”. 「英語ができます」 means you know English; 「英語が上手です」 means you speak it well (not something to say about yourself).

meaning: Add 「の」 after a verb to turn the action into a noun, then add 「好き」, 「上手」 and so on to say you like or are good at doing something.
connection: Verb dictionary form + のが + 好き／嫌い／上手／下手, etc.

senses.label: Like / dislike doing
senses.meaning: A verb can't be followed directly by 「が好き」. First add 「の」 to make it a noun.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + のが + 好き／嫌い
examples: I like reading books.
I hate getting up early in the morning.

senses.label: Good / bad at doing
senses.meaning: Says someone does something well or badly. About yourself, 「得意」 and 「苦手」 are common.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + のが + 上手／下手／得意／苦手
examples: My mother is good at cooking.
I'm not good at speaking in front of people.

senses.label: Speed of an action
senses.meaning: Describes how fast someone does something.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + のが + 速い／早い／遅い
examples: My younger brother runs fast.
My father eats quickly.

notes: A verb can't connect directly to 「が好き」: ✕「読むが好き」 → ○「読むのが好き」.
The object inside the clause still takes 「を」: ✕「本が読むのが好き」 → ○「本を読むのが好き」.
Telling someone to their face 「〜のが下手ですね」 is rude. When talking about what you're not good at, 「〜のが苦手です」 sounds more natural and tactful.
The 「の」 in 「赤いのが好き」 stands in for a noun (“the red one”) and isn't this grammar point: 「走るのが好き」 = I like running; 「赤いのが好き」 = I like the red one.

etymology: 「の」 was originally a particle showing possession. It later developed into a formal noun that can follow a verb so the whole action is used as a noun.
formation: The object of na-adjectives like 「好き」 and 「上手」 must be a noun, marked as 「noun＋が」. To make an action the object, you first have to turn it into a noun: add the formal noun 「の」 after the verb's dictionary form, 「読む」 → 「読むの」 (“the act of reading”). So 「本を読むのが好き」 = [「本を読む」＋「の」] (the act of reading books) ＋「が」＋「好き」. 「の」 just packages the whole clause into a noun and leaves its inner structure unchanged, so the object inside still takes 「を」. 「の」 leans toward concrete, first-hand actions, which is also why it sounds more conversational and everyday than 「こと」.

similar.title: 〜が好き・〜が嫌い・〜が上手・〜が下手
similar.explanation: Same origin: it uses the same 「好き・上手」. When the object is a noun, say 「Nが好き」 directly; when it's an action, use 「Vのが好き」.

similar.title: 〜の (nominalizer)
similar.explanation: Same origin: it's the very 「の」 that turns the action into a noun in this pattern. At N4 its other uses, such as 「のを」 and 「のは」, are covered systematically: 「鳥が鳴くのを聞いた」.

similar.title: 〜こと (nominalizer)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and mostly interchangeable: 「読むことが好き」 and 「読むのが好き」 mean basically the same; 「こと」 is more written and abstract. For concrete actions you see or hear directly (「〜のを見る」, 「〜のが聞こえる」), only 「の」 works.
